title: Onboard horizon sensitivity report: batching, cache, max_tokens
body:
Purpose
This doc summarizes an onboarding-focused sweep exploring the latency/cost/quality tradeoffs across batching, cache modes, and max_tokens limits. The goal: produce a pragmatic default config for new-model onboarding runs and detect regressions that would materially impact PLG user experience. This is intentionally focused on realistic prompt distributions (onboard-suite-v2) rather than synthetic single-shot prompts.

Context & Motivation
- Recent customer signups show sensitivity to tail latency (P95) when run with default autoscaling and default inference settings.
- Our onboarding eval harness runs model-quality checks + smoke load tests; these runs have grown expensive and occasionally reveal quality regressions when we tune quantization/batching aggressively.
- We need clear knobs and a set of safe defaults that balance cost and latency while preserving eval pass rates for the typical prompt mixes we see in onboarding.

Experiment matrix
- Dataset / promptset: onboard-suite-v2 (~12k prompts, mixed short/med/long; 40% reused prefixes, 25% multi-turn).
- Models: base-open-13B (fp16), quant-4bit-open-13B (int4) for a subset.
- Hardware: A100-80GB (rt-3.8.1) and H100 (rt-3.9.0-wip) for comparative runs.
- Runtime params varied: batch_size = [1, 4, 8, 16, 32], cache_mode = [none, prefix, kv], max_tokens = [64, 128, 256, 512].
- Concurrency: 1, 8, 32 concurrent clients (steady arrival).
- Trials: 3 seeds per configuration; each run executes full promptset to capture quality metrics.

Measured signals
- Latency: P50 and P95 per-request (wall clock), and per-token parsing overhead.
- Throughput: tokens/sec aggregated across workers.
- Cost proxy: effective token-cost-per-1M (runtime-time * GPU-node $/hr normalized) and CPU overhead.
- Quality: eval pass rate on downstream checks from onboarding harness (functional correctness rules, hallucination filters, scalar QA score).
- Observability: cache hit ratio, KV cache eviction rate, batching distribution, queueing time.

Key results (summary)
1) Batch size sweet spot depends on latency SLO: batch=8 gives best cost/latency balance for P50-sensitive workloads. At batch=8 we saw 18–28% cost reduction vs batch=1, P95 penalty <12% in typical concurrency (<=8).
2) Large batches (batch>=16) reduce unit cost more but introduce tail latency spikes under bursty arrival; P95 increases up to 60% on A100 and 40% on H100. For PLG onboarding runs (which must feel snappy), batch>=16 is risky unless combined with strict queue-time SLOs or warm-started reserved capacity.
3) Prefix caching yields consistent P95 improvements when promptset has high prefix reuse (>25%). For onboard-suite-v2, prefix cache reduced average inference work by ~22% and P95 by ~15% at identical batch settings. However, effectiveness collapses if max_tokens is changed to force completions that diverge (long completions).
4) KV caching helps for multi-turn prompts: with kv enabled for multi-turn subset, tokens/sec improved and P95 dropped ~12% compared to no-kv on identical batch sizes. But KV cache memory pressure caused eviction cascades at high concurrency for large max_tokens; eviction spikes correlated with P95 jitter.
5) max_tokens tradeoff: increasing max_tokens from 128->512 increases average cost by 1.8x (approx linear) and increases chance of quality improving on long-context tasks (small but measurable ∆quality +2–3% pass rate). For short/medium prompts, higher max_tokens mostly wastes compute; recommend conservative defaults.
6) Quantized model (int4) reduces cost by ~38% but showed a marginal drop in eval pass rate (avg -1.4% absolute). When combined with batch>=8, some tasks saw more quality variance; so flagging quantized variants in onboarding is warranted.

Interesting failure modes / anomalies
- Cache eviction cascades: On A100 with kv + batch=32 + max_tokens=512 we observed eviction churn: sudden drop in cache hit ratio from 78%->19% under concurrency=32. That aligned with P95 spikes and >1 minute tail outliers. Root cause looks like memory accounting bug in runtime kernel selection under quantized path (filed PR referenced).
- Queueing vs batching interplay: naive autoscalers that increased worker count during bursts allowed batch sizes to grow without queue-time caps, which paradoxically increased P95. Need a queue-time throttle or per-route max_batch_window config.

Practical recommendations (defaults for onboarding harness)
- Default onboarding profile: batch_size=8, cache_mode=prefix (enabled), max_tokens=256, concurrency cap per-run=16. Rationale: preserves snappy P95 while reducing cost; robust across A100/H100.
- For multi-turn-heavy promptsets: enable kv cache but run a preflight memory check (eviction threshold alert at 10% hit-ratio-drop).
- Avoid quantized variants as the default for initial onboarding quality checks; add an explicit quantized-check stage that runs after base-pass to measure quality deltas.
- Add a max-batch-window config (e.g., 20ms) for onboarding harness runs to avoid excessive queueing-induced P95 spikes.

Regression checks to add to CI/harness
- Latency regression: new model onboarding must not regress P95 by >15% vs seed baseline at batch=8,prefix,max_tokens=256.
- Cost regression: unit-cost-per-1M-tokens must be reported and not exceed 1.4x of baseline without explicit opt-in.
- Quality regression: eval pass rate drop >2% should block automated onboarding promotion and open a triage ticket.

Action items & Owners
- Add these defaults to onboarding DAG and update quickstart: owner Rahul Desai (due 2025-09-26).
- Create automated eviction-alert rule in console for onboarding runs: owner Maya Chen (due 2025-09-22).
- Merge runtime PR to fix memory accounting in quantized kernel selection: see PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/829; owner Liam O'Connor (in-progress).
- Add a quantized-check gating step and a docs note about expected quality delta: owner Nina Alvarez (due 2025-09-30).

Notes for SRE / infra
- If we keep batch=8 default, reserve a small warm pool for onboarding runs to absorb bursts without autoscaler-induced increases in batch window. This reduces queueing jitter without large cost.
- Consider exposing per-route max_batch_window in the console with a 0-100ms slider for customer tuning.

Appendix: representative numbers (A100, batch=1/8/16, prefix enabled, max_tokens=256, concurrency=8)
- batch=1: P50 85ms, P95 290ms, tokens/sec 12k, cost-per-1M tokens = $1200 (proxy), eval pass rate = 92.1%
- batch=8: P50 120ms, P95 320ms, tokens/sec 45k, cost-per-1M tokens = $905, eval pass rate = 91.9%
- batch=16: P50 160ms, P95 475ms, tokens/sec 68k, cost-per-1M tokens = $720, eval pass rate = 91.7%

Closing thought
Onboarding is a special workload: it mixes human-facing latency expectations with noisy eval-quality signals. The goal is not to squeeze every last cent out of cost, but to keep onboarding fast and reliable while surfacing quality regressions early. The defaults above are intentionally conservative; once a model passes the base quality gates we can run additional cost-optimization passes (larger batch, quantized) in a separate stage.

If you want, I can extract these recommendations into a short one-pager for Console defaults and create the PRs for the CI checks.
